title: 2001 HMMT February Advanced Topics Problem 10
statement: Alex picks his favorite point \((x, y)\) in the first quadrant on the unit circle \(x^{2}+y^{2}=1\), such that a ray from the origin through \((x, y)\) is \(\theta\) radians counterclockwise from the positive \(x\)-axis. He then computes \(\cos ^{-1}\left(\frac{4 x+3 y}{5}\right)\) and is surprised to get \(\theta\). What is \(\tan (\theta)\) ?

solutions.text: \(x=\cos (\theta), y=\sin (\theta)\). By the trig identity you never thought you'd need, \(\frac{4 x+3 y}{5}=\cos (\theta-\phi)\), where \(\phi\) has sine \(3 / 5\) and cosine \(4 / 5\). Now \(\theta-\phi=\theta\) is impossible, since \(\phi \neq 0\), so we must have \(\theta-\phi=-\theta\), hence \(\theta=\phi / 2\). Now use the trusty half-angle identities to get \(\tan (\theta)=\frac{1}{3}\).
